title.en: Prince Ousu Steals His Father's Brides

summary.en: Emperor Keiko, hearing of the beauty of two sisters, sends his son Prince Oho-usu (the young Yamato-takeru) to summon them to court. The prince instead weds both sisters himself and sends up other women under their names.
summary.zh: 景行天皇聞二女之美，遣王子小碓命召之入宮。王子竟自娶二女，而以他人冒名送入。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Emperor Oho-tarashi-hiko (Keiko) had heard wondrous reports of the beauty of the sisters Ye-hime and Oto-hime, daughters of King Kamu-oho-ne, ancestor of the Rulers of the Land of Minu. To see them for himself he sent his own son, the fierce Prince Oho-usu, with the errand of summoning the two maidens up to the capital.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 290-291 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The prince did not carry out the command. Instead of sending the sisters to his father, he took both maidens to wife himself. Then, so that his deceit should not be discovered, he sought out other women, falsely gave them the two sisters' names, and sent them up to the capital in their place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 290-291 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign, knowing the women who arrived to be substitutes and not the beauties he had asked for, looked long upon them again and again with longing; yet he never wedded them, and so they were made to sorrow. From Ye-hime the prince begot King Oshi-kuro-no-ye-hiko, and from Oto-hime King Oshi-kuro-no-oto-hiko.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 290-291 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Prince Ousu Crushes His Elder Brother

summary.en: Ordered by his father to make his lazy elder brother attend the royal meals, Prince Ousu instead seizes him in the privy, crushes and tears him apart, and flings the limbs away. Terrified by his son's ferocity, the emperor sends him against the Kumaso brigands.
summary.zh: 天皇命小碓命勸兄赴朝夕御膳。小碓竟於廁中捕兄，折裂其肢而棄之。天皇懼其凶猛，乃遣其西征熊襲。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign asked his younger son, Prince Wo-usu: 'Why does your elder brother not come forth to the morning and evening great august repasts? Take the trouble to teach him his duty.' Yet five days passed and the elder prince still did not appear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 291-292 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Asked again how he had taken the trouble, the younger prince answered flatly: 'In the early morning, when he went into the privy, I grasped hold of him and crushed him, and, pulling off his limbs, wrapped them in matting and flung them away.' He had killed his own elder brother with his bare hands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 291-292 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Alarmed at the valour and ferocity of his child's disposition, the emperor resolved to turn that violence outward. 'In the West there are two Kumaso bravoes, unsubmissive and disrespectful men. So take them,' he commanded, and thus he sent the prince off on the campaign that would make him Yamato-takeru.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 291-292 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Yamato-takeru Slays the Kumaso Bravoes in a Girl's Dress

region.zh: 熊襲之地（九州，象徵座標）

summary.en: Sent west against two unsubmissive Kumaso bravoes, Prince Wo-usu disguises himself as a girl in his aunt Yamato-hime's clothing, infiltrates their feast, and stabs them both. The dying elder bravo, acknowledging no one braver in the west, bestows on him the name Yamato-take.
summary.zh: 小碓命奉命西征熊襲二豪傑，借姨倭姬命之衣女装，混入宴席刺殺之。垂死之兄豪傑讚其勇，賜名日本武尊。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Sent west to destroy the two Kumaso bravoes, the young prince first prayed at the shrines. His aunt, Her Augustness Yamato-hime, priestess of Ise, granted him her own august upper garment and skirt, and he set out with a sabre hidden in his bosom. Reaching the bravoes' cave, ringed with a three-fold belt of warriors, he found a feast being prepared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 292-294 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the day of the rejoicing he combed down his bound hair after the manner of girls, put on his aunt's garment and skirt, and, looking quite like a young girl, stood amid the women inside the cave. The two brothers, delighted with the supposed maiden, set her between them and rejoiced exuberantly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 292-294 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the feast was at its height the prince drew the hidden sabre, seized the elder bravo by the collar, and thrust the blade through his chest; the younger fled, but was caught at the foot of the steps and stabbed through the buttock. 'Do not move the sword; I have something to say,' the wounded bravo begged, and told him: no one in the west is so brave as we two, yet in Great Yamato there is a man braver still - take, then, the name Yamato-take.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 292-294 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The moment the bravo finished speaking, the prince ripped him up like a ripe melon. Thenceforward he was praised as His Augustness Yamato-take. Returning to the capital he subdued and pacified every deity of the mountains, rivers, and Anado on his way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 292-294 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Wooden-Sword Trick at Izumo

summary.en: Wishing to slay the Izumo bravo, Yamato-takeru pretends friendship, secretly girds a false sword of oak, and proposes an exchange of blades after bathing. When the bravo cannot draw the wooden sword, Yamato-takeru cuts him down.
summary.zh: 倭建命欲誅出雲豪傑，偽結盟好，密佩櫟木假劍。浴於斐伊川後，提議互換佩劍；出雲豪傑拔不出木劍，遂被斬殺。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Entering the Land of Izumo, Yamato-takeru wished to slay the Izumo bravo. On arriving he bound himself to the man in friendship, and secretly shaped an oak tree into a false sword, girded it on, and went with the bravo to bathe in the River Hi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 294-295 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: He got out of the river first, took up the real sword the bravo had laid down and girded it on himself, saying 'Let us exchange swords!' The unsuspecting bravo, climbing out after him, drew on Yamato-takeru's wooden imitation without noticing the difference.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 294-295 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Come on! Let us cross swords,' Yamato-takeru suggested. The Izumo bravo could not draw the false blade. Instantly Yamato-takeru drew his own sword and slew him, singing a triumphal song; so he extirpated the bravoes, made the land orderly, and went up to report to the Heavenly Sovereign.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 294-295 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Herb-Quelling Sabre and the Suruga Fire

summary.en: Sent east against the twelve roads, Yamato-takeru visits Ise, where his aunt Yamato-hime gives him the Herb-Quelling Sabre and a bag with a fire-striker inside. In Sagamu a lying ruler sets fire to the moor around him; he mows the grass with the sword, strikes a counter-fire, escapes, and destroys the rulers, giving the place its name Yakidzu.
summary.zh: 倭建命東征，於伊勢受姨倭姬命賜草薙劍與火石囊。駿河國主縱火燒野，倭建命以劍刈草，擊石取火，燃逆火突圍，盡誅國主，其地遂名燒津。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Again the emperor commanded Yamato-takeru to subdue the savage deities and unsubmissive people of the twelve roads of the East, giving him no army. Going into the temple of the Great Deity of Ise, he wept to his aunt Yamato-hime that his father must surely think he would die quickly. She bestowed on him the Herb-Quelling Sabre and an august bag, saying: 'If there should be an emergency, open the mouth of the bag.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 295-297 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the Land of Wohari he plighted his troth to Princess Miyadzu, promising to wed her on his return, then pushed into the eastern lands and pacified their savage deities. Reaching Sagamu, its ruler lied that a violent deity dwelt in the middle of a great moor; when Yamato-takeru entered the moor to see it, the ruler set the dry grass ablaze around him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 295-297 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Knowing he was deceived, he opened the bag: inside was a fire-striker. First he mowed away the surrounding herbage with his august sword, then struck fire and kindled a counter-fire that burnt the herbage and drove back the flames, and he returned forth alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 295-297 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he took vengeance: he killed and destroyed all the Rulers of that land and set fire to them, so that the place is called Yakidzu, the burning. Thus the Herb-Quelling Sabre earned its name by mowing the grass that would have destroyed its bearer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 295-297 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Oto-tachibana Enters the Sea; the Naming of Adzuma
title.zh: 弟橘媛投海與東國得名

region.en: Hashirimizu crossing, Tokyo Bay, Japan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 走水海峽（東京灣，象徵座標）

summary.en: At the Hashiri-midzu crossing a sea deity raises waves against Yamato-takeru's ship. His empress Oto-tachibana seats herself on eight thicknesses of rugs spread on the water and enters the sea in his stead, calming the waves. Seven days later her comb drifts ashore and is buried. At the Ashigara pass a white deer is struck down and the pass named Adzuma.
summary.zh: 走水渡海時，海神興浪阻船。弟橘媛於浪上鋪八重席而投海代君，浪立平。七日後其梳漂至海濱，葬為陵。足柄峠白鹿被擊斃，其地遂名阿豆摩（東）。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Penetrating eastward, Yamato-takeru crossed the sea of Hashiri-midzu. The deity of that crossing raised the waves, tossing the ship so that it could not proceed. Then his empress, Her Augustness Princess Oto-tachibana, spoke: 'I will enter the sea instead of the august child. The august child must complete the service on which he has been sent, and take back a report to the Heavenly Sovereign.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 297-299 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: As she was about to enter the sea she spread eight thicknesses of sedge rugs, eight of skin rugs and eight of silk rugs on the top of the waves, and sat down upon them. At once the violent waves went down, and the august ship was able to proceed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 297-299 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seven days afterwards the empress's august comb drifted onto the sea-beach; it was taken and placed in an august mausoleum built for her. Yamato-takeru pushed on, subdued all the savage Yemishi and the deities of the mountains and rivers, and turned homeward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 297-299 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the foot of the Ashigara pass he was eating his provisions when the deity of the pass, transformed into a white deer, stood before him; he struck it with a scrap of wild chive and it died, hit in the eye. Mounting the pass he sighed three times and cried 'Adzuma ha ya!' - oh my wife! - and so that land is called Adzuma, the East.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 297-299 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Deity of Mount Ibuki and Yamato-takeru's Death
title.zh: 伊吹山神與倭建命之死

summary.en: Honouring the old fire-lighter Sakawori and wedding Princess Miyazu, Yamato-takeru leaves his Grass-Quelling Sabre in her house and goes empty-handed to take the deity of Mount Ibuki. A white boar - the deity's messenger - is spared but his boastful insolence brings ice-rain that breaks him; his legs fail, he sings land-regretting songs and dies at the moor of Nobo.
summary.zh: 倭建命嘉獎老火夫佐川折，娶美夜務媛，留草薙劍於其家，空手征伊吹山神。見白豬而口出狂言，山神降雹雨擊之；腿如船舵不能行，沿途嘆歌，至能褒野而死。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Crossing into Kahi, Yamato-takeru dwelt in the palace of Sakawori, the old man who had been the lighter of the august fire; the prince praised him and bestowed on him the Rulership of the Eastern Lands. He then subdued the deity of the Shinanu pass, and in Wohari went to the house of Princess Miyazu, to whom he had plighted his troth; seeing her menstruation, he sang, cohabited with her, and left the Grass-Quelling Sabre in her house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 300-302 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he went to take the deity of Mount Ibuki, declaring he would take him empty-handed. On the mountain-side a white boar the size of a bull met him. 'This creature transformed into a white boar must be a messenger from the deity. Though I slay it not now, I will slay it when I return,' he said, and ascended, insolently sparing it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 302-303 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The deity punished his boast: heavy ice-rain fell, striking and perplexing him. Descending, he rested at the fresh spring of Tama-kura-be and his heart awoke somewhat; but at the moor of Tagi his legs had become rudder-shaped, unable to walk. He leaned on an august staff at the Tsuwe-tsuki pass, found his forgotten sword still at the single pine of Cape Wotsu, and sang at the village of Mihe that his legs were like three-fold crooks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 303-305 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Reaching the moor of Nobo, he regretted his native land, singing that he longed for Yamato with its green layers of trees, for his wife and children. His sickness became very urgent; as soon as he finished singing his final song, he died. A courier was despatched to the Heavenly Sovereign to announce his death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 305-306 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The White Bird of Yamato-takeru's Tomb

summary.en: At Yamato-takeru's funeral his empresses and children build a mausoleum and crawl through the rice-fields sobbing songs. The dead prince becomes a white dotterel eight fathoms long and soars to heaven; they pursue it through stubble and sea, singing the four songs still sung at imperial burials, and bury him at Shiki in Kawachi - yet the bird flies up to heaven again.
summary.zh: 倭建命葬禮上，后妃皇子筑陵而匍匐歌哭。死者化為八尋白鳥沖天，眾人踏芒入海追之而歌；其四歌至今天皇大葬時皆詠之。葬於河内志幾，白鳥再度沖天而去。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When word of Yamato-takeru's death reached the capital, his empresses and august children dwelling in Yamato went down and built an august mausoleum, crawling hither and thither through the rice-fields surrounding it and sobbing out songs of grief over his grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 306-308 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the dead prince turned into a white dotterel eight fathoms long and, soaring up to heaven, flew off towards the shore. The mourners tore their feet treading the bamboo-grass stubble yet forgot the pain, pursuing him with lamentations across the fields and out into the salt sea as the bird flew and perched on the seaside.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 306-308 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The four songs sung at that chase are sung to this day at the great august interment of a Heavenly Sovereign. The bird flew on to Shiki in the land of Kafuchi, where another mausoleum was made and Yamato-takeru laid to rest - the Mausoleum of the White-Bird. Nevertheless the bird soared up thence to heaven again and flew away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 306-308 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Yamato-takeru: The Kuwagata Hero Cycle
title.zh: 日本武尊英雄紀：從熊襲到白鳥

region.en: Yamato (Nara) to eastern Japan, Kojiki hero cycle (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大和至東國（倭建命巡歷，象徵座標）

summary.en: Flagship deep record: the full Kojiki cycle of Yamato-takeru, from his fratricidal youth and the Kumaso trick that earned his name, through the Herb-Quelling Sabre and the Suruga fire, Oto-tachibana's sacrifice at sea, the naming of Adzuma, and the ice-rain punishment of Mount Ibuki, to his death songs at Nobo and apotheosis as the white bird.
summary.zh: 本紀全錄《古事記》倭建命一生：弑兄、熊襲女裝得號、草薙劍與駿河火、弟橘媛投海、東國得名、伊吹山雹雨懲罰、能褒野絕命之歌與白鳥升天。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); the hero is woven into imperial genealogy, so this record is handled as sacred-legendary material, presented as condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Ordered to make his negligent elder brother attend the royal meals, the young Prince Wo-usu crushed him in the privy and tore off his limbs. Alarmed at such ferocity, Emperor Keiko sent him west to take the two Kumaso bravoes. Dressing in his aunt Yamato-hime's garments as a girl, he infiltrated their feast, stabbed both brothers, and heard the dying elder name him Yamato-take - the one braver than any man of the west.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 291-294 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: With a false wooden sword he tricked and slew the Izumo bravo. Sent east without an army - and certain his father meant him to die - he received from Yamato-hime at Ise the Herb-Quelling Sabre and a bag. When the ruler of Sagamu fired the moor around him, the bag's fire-striker let him mow the grass, strike a counter-fire, and burn his deceivers in their own flames: the place is Yakidzu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 294-297 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the Hashiri-midzu crossing the sea deity raised deadly waves, and his empress Oto-tachibana, seated on eight thicknesses of rugs spread on the water, gave her life to the sea in his stead; her comb, drifting ashore seven days later, was buried as a mausoleum. Sighing 'Adzuma ha ya' - oh my wife - at the Ashigara pass, he gave the East its name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 297-299 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Homeward, he honoured the old fire-lighter Sakawori, wed Princess Miyazu and left the Grass-Quelling Sabre in her house - whence it came to rest at the shrine of Atsuta - then went empty-handed against the deity of Mount Ibuki. A white boar, the deity's messenger, he insolently promised to slay later; the deity answered with ice-rain that broke his legs to rudders. Dragging himself from pass to moor he sang his land-regretting songs, and died at Nobo as the last song ended.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 300-306 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

narrative.en:
Yamato-takeru is the Kojiki's great tragic hero, and his cycle begins in blood. When Emperor Keiko asks why his eldest son never comes to the morning and evening meals, he orders the younger prince, Wo-usu, to teach him his duty. Wo-usu's answer is to seize his brother in the privy, crush him, tear off his limbs, and wrap them in matting. Horrified by his son's ferocity, the emperor redirects it outward: two unsubmissive Kumaso bravoes in the west must be taken.

For this errand the prince's aunt Yamato-hime, priestess of Ise, gives him her own upper garment and skirt. Binding his hair like a girl's, hiding a sabre in his bosom, he waits until the day of the bravoes' feast, slips into their cave among the women, and is set between the delighted brothers as if he were a beautiful girl. At the height of the feast he draws the blade, stabs the elder through the chest, runs down the younger and pierces his buttock. Dying, the bravo offers him a name: no men in the west are braver than they two, yet in Great Yamato there is one braver still - so let him be praised as Yamato-take. The prince rips him up like a ripe melon, and the name Yamato-takeru stays with him forever. A second trick follows at Izumo, where he girds a wooden imitation of a sword, exchanges blades with the unsuspecting bravo after a bath in the River Hi, and cuts down the man who cannot draw his own weapon.

The third command is the fatal one: pacify the twelve roads of the East, without an army. Yamato-takeru weeps at Ise that his father must think he will die quickly, and Yamato-hime grants him the Herb-Quelling Sabre and a bag he must open in emergency. After plighting troth with Princess Miyadzu of Wohari, he reaches Sagamu, whose ruler lies that a violent deity dwells in the middle of a moor; once the prince is inside, the ruler fires the dry grass. Out of the bag comes a fire-striker: he mows the herbage with the sacred sword, strikes fire, kindles a counter-fire that drives back the flames, escapes, and burns the deceivers alive - giving Yakidzu, the Burning, its name.

At the crossing of Hashiri-midzu the sea deity heaps up waves no ship can ride. His empress, Princess Oto-tachibana, resolves to enter the sea in her husband's place so that he may finish his service; she spreads eight thicknesses of sedge, skin and silk rugs upon the waves, sits down on them, and the storm subsides. Seven days later her comb drifts to the beach and is buried in a mausoleum of its own. On his return he slays a white deer that is the deity of the Ashigara pass, sighs three times - 'Adzuma ha ya!' oh my wife - and names the whole East Adzuma. In Kahi he honours the fire-lighter Sakawori with the rulership of the Eastern Lands; in Wohari he weds Princess Miyazu, and leaves the Grass-Quelling Sabre in her house, from which it passes into the keeping of the Atsuta shrine.

Then comes his undoing at Mount Ibuki. Boasting that he will take its deity empty-handed, he meets a white boar the size of a bull, recognizes it as the deity's messenger, and insolently says he will slay it on his way back. The deity replies with heavy ice-rain. His legs grow rudder-shaped and will not carry him; he names the places of his suffering - Tagi, Tsuwe-tsuki, Mihe - leaning on a staff, finding a forgotten sword whole at Cape Wotsu, and singing songs of regret for Yamato, its layered green trees, his wife and his children. At the moor of Nobo, as his final song ends, he dies.

His empresses and children build his mausoleum and crawl through the rice-fields about it, sobbing. Then the dead prince becomes a white dotterel eight fathoms long and soars toward heaven; they pursue it through stubble and sea, and the four songs of that chase are sung at every imperial burial to this day. He is laid to rest at Shiki in Kawachi, in the Mausoleum of the White-Bird - but the bird rises once more and flies to heaven, leaving the tomb empty. The cycle closes with genealogy: his sons carry the imperial line onward, and the hero who slew gods' messengers and enemies of the realm ends as a bird crossing the boundary between Yamato and the sky.
narrative.zh: 此為《古事記》所載日本武尊之完整英雄紀：弑兄而畏、女装誅熊襲而得尊號、木劍誅出雲豪傑、伊勢受草薙劍與火石囊、駿河野火中刈草逆燒、弟橘媛鋪八重席投海平浪、足柄峠嘆而名東、伊吹山白豬口出狂言遭雹雨、腿如船舵、能褒野絕命之歌、化八尋白鳥沖天，葬於河内志幾白鳥陵，其四歌至今用於天皇大葬。

functions: Explains the origin of the hero's name Yamato-takeru and of the place-name Adzuma for eastern Japan, binding geography to heroic narrative.
Etiologizes the Grass-Mowing (Herb-Quelling) Sword's cult at Atsuta shrine and the fire-escape rites associated with it.
Provides the canonical funeral songs sung at the burial of Japanese sovereigns, ritualizing imperial death as transformation into a bird.
Models the ideal of the unflinching sacrificial prince whose consort's self-offering calms the sea, a paradigm of loyalty in later Japanese literature.
