title.en: The Deity Rebukes Emperor Chuuai

summary.en: At Kashii in Tsukushi, preparing to attack the Kumaso, Chuuai plays his lute while Take-uchi asks the divine will. His empress Jingu, divinely possessed, announces a treasure-land to the west; the emperor disbelieves and falls silent, the deities declare the land is not his to rule, and he dies as the lute's sound dies. A great purification follows, and the oracle repeats: the child in her womb will rule this land and the westward one.
summary.zh: 仲哀天皇在筑紫香椎宮，欲討熊襲，命武內宿禰奏神意。神功皇后神靈憑依，宣示西方寶國；天皇不信，坐而沉默，諸神怒言其不堪治此國，天皇遂於琴音絕處崩殂。其後大祓，神諭重申：腹中皇子將治此國與西方之國。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In this reign Heir Apparent Homuda-wake was born to Empress Okinaga-tarashi, named Oho-tomo-wake for the flesh like an elbow-pad on his newborn arm - a sign, known while he was still in the womb, that he would rule countries; and the granaries of Ahaji were established. Then the emperor, dwelling at the palace of Kashihi in Tsukushi, was about to smite the land of Kumaso: he played on his august lute while the Prime Minister, the Noble Take-uchi, stood in the pure court requesting the divine orders.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 313-316 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Empress, divinely possessed, charged him with this counsel: 'There is a land to the Westward, and in that land is abundance of various treasures dazzling to the eye, from gold and silver downwards. I will now bestow this land upon thee.' The Heavenly Sovereign replied that from a high place looking west one sees no country - only the great sea - and, saying the deities lie, pushed away his lute, sat silent, and would not play.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 315-316 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the deities were very angry: 'Altogether this empire is not a land over which thou oughtest to rule. Do thou go to the one road!' Take-uchi begged him to continue playing; he drew the lute slowly and languidly played - and almost immediately the sound became inaudible. Lifting a light, they found the Heavenly Sovereign dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 315-316 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Astonished and alarmed, they set him in a mortuary palace and made a great purification, seeking out all crimes - flaying alive and backwards, breaking rice-field divisions, filling ditches, fouling, and unions of superiors and inferiors, with horses, cattle, fowls and dogs. Take-uchi again requested the divine command, and the answer was the same: this land is to be ruled by the august child in the empress's womb, a male child, by the doing of the Great Heaven-Shining Deity and the three Possessing-Male deities.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 316-317 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Empress Jingu's Conquest of Shiragi

summary.en: Following the deities' instructions, Empress Jingu scatters podocarpus ashes, chopsticks and chopped wands on the waves as sea-charms, and her fleet crosses on the backs of the fish of the sea-plain. The wave pushes up into the middle of Shiragi; its chieftain surrenders, promising horses and tribute forever, and Jingu plants her staff on his gate and installs the Rough August Spirits of Sumiye as guardians before returning.
summary.zh: 神功皇后依神敕，以竹木灰、箸、折枝散於海波為呪具，海中大小魚類負舟而渡，順風直入新羅國中。新羅王懼而降服，永為馬飼與貢船之國；皇后插御杖於其門，立住吉荒魂為鎮守神，而後歸國。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); this is a legendary conquest narrative with later nationalist readings, handled here as myth via public-domain paraphrase for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The deities instructed: present offerings to all the Heavenly, Earthly, mountain, river and sea deities, set the august spirits on the top of the vessel, put the ashes of the podocarpus tree into gourds, and make quantities of chopsticks and chopped material, scattering them all on the waves of the great sea so as to cross over. Jingu punctually fulfilled these instructions, equipped an army and marshalled her vessels.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 317-318 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: As she crossed, the fish of the sea-plain, both great and small, bore the august vessel across on their backs, a strong favourable wind arose, and the vessel followed the billows. The wave of the august vessel pushed up onto the land of Shiragi, reaching the middle of the country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 317-318 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chieftain of the country, alarmed and trembling, petitioned: 'From this time forward, obedient to the Heavenly Sovereign's commands, I will feed his august horses and will marshal vessels every year, never letting their keels or poles and oars dry, and will respectfully serve him without drawing back while heaven and earth shall last.' So Shiragi was made the feeder of the august horses and Kudara the crossing store.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 318-319 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Empress stuck her august staff on the gate of the chieftain of Shiragi, made the Rough August Spirits of the Great Deities of the Inlet of Sumiye the guardian deities of the land, laid them to rest, and crossed back to Tsukushi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 318-319 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Jingu Binds the Stone; the Birth at Umi
title.zh: 神功皇后束石生譽田別

summary.en: While the conquest of Shiragi is yet unfinished and the empress is heavy with child, she binds a stone about her skirt to restrain her womb, crosses back to Tsukushi, and gives birth at the place called Umi. At Tamashima she sits on a midstream shoal, picks threads from her skirt, and hooks trout with grains of rice - a custom still kept by women of the first decade of the fourth moon.
summary.zh: 征新羅事未竟而皇后有孕，乃取石繫於裙腰以束胎，渡歸筑紫，於宇美之地誕皇子。又於玉島里坐川中洲，抽裙線以米粒釣鱸，至今四月上旬婦女釣鱸之俗由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: While the business of Shiragi was yet unconcluded, the child with which the Empress Okinaga-tarashi was pregnant was about to be born. To restrain her august womb she took a stone and wound it round the waist of her august skirt, and so went on with the campaign; the stone is still to be seen at the village of Ito in the Land of Tsukushi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 319-320 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Only after she had crossed back to the Land of Tsukushi was the august child born, and the place was given the name Umi - the birth. The future emperor Homuda-wake had been carried through a foreign campaign in his mother's womb.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 319-320 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Later, reaching the village of Tamashima in the Department of Matsura in the first decade of the fourth moon, she partook of an august meal on the river bank, then sat on a shoal in the middle of the river, picked out threads from her august skirt, used grains of rice as bait, and hooked the trout. Down to the present time women in the first decade of the fourth moon pick threads from their skirts, use grains as bait, and hook trout after her example.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 320 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mourning-Vessel Ruse: Kagosaka and Oshikuma
title.zh: 喪船之計：香坂王與忍熊王之亂

summary.en: Returning to Yamato, Jingu spreads a rumour that her newborn prince is dead, setting her child in a mourning-vessel. The princes Kagosaka and Oshikuma rise in revolt; a boar devours Kagosaka during an omen hunt; Oshikuma's forces are broken by a false-surrender trick of snapping bowstrings, and the prince and his general plunge together into the sea singing.
summary.zh: 神功皇后歸大和，恐人心不服，設喪船載皇子而謠傳皇子已死。香坂王、忍熊王聞而叛；香坂王出獵占兆，遭大豬連根拔櫟樹吞之。忍熊王據兵相抗，武內宿禰之將折弦詐降，敵解弓而遭伏擊潰敗；忍熊王與將領伊佐比臣同赴海而歌，相抱投海而死。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Returning up to Yamato, Princess Okinaga-tarashi, doubting the disposition of the people, prepared a mourning-vessel, set the august child in it, and let a report ooze out that the child was already dead. King Kagosaka and King Oshikuma, sons of the late emperor, heard of it and thought to waylay her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 321-322 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the moor of Toga they hunted for an omen: King Kagosaka climbed an oak-tree, whereupon a large angry boar came forth, dug up the tree, and devoured him. His younger brother Oshikuma, undaunted, raised an army to close with the mourning-vessel as an empty vessel.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 321-322 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: An army was landed from the mourning-vessel and fought the rebels back to Yamashiro, where both sides stood without retreating. Then Take-furu-kuma planned: it was spread abroad that the Empress was already dead and there was no need for further fighting, and his men snapped their bowstrings, feigning submission. Believing the falsehood, Oshikuma's men unbent their bows and put away their arms - whereupon the empress's troops drew prepared bowstrings from their topknots, re-stretched their bows, and pursued and smote them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 321-322 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The rebels rallied at Afusaka and were defeated again at Sasanami. King Oshikuma and the Noble Isahi, pursued and pressed, got aboard a vessel, floated on the sea, sang a song of their fate, and together plunged into the water and died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 322-323 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Name-Exchange Deity and the Broken-Nosed Dolphins
title.zh: 伊紗自氣神換名與海豚獻食

summary.en: Taking the Heir Apparent Homuda-wake for purification through Afumi and Wakasa, Take-uchi halts at Tsunuga, where the local deity Izasa-wake appears in a dream asking to exchange names. The shore is found lined with broken-nosed dolphin-fishes as the deity's thank-offering, the child grants him the name Great Deity of August Food, and the blood-stinking strand is called Chiura.
summary.zh: 武內宿禰攜譽田別皇子經近江、若狹行祓，宿於敦賀。伊紗自氣神夜夢求與皇子換名，翌晨海濱盡是破鼻海豚，為神之謝禮。皇子賜神名「御食津神」，海豚鼻血腥臭之浦遂名血浦，今稱敦賀。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Noble Take-uchi, taking with him the Heir Apparent for the purpose of purification, passed through the lands of Afumi and Wakasa and built a temporary palace at Tsunuga at the mouth of the Road of Koshi for the child to dwell in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 323-324 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: There the Great Deity Izasa-wake, who dwelt in that place, appeared at night in a dream: 'I wish to exchange my name for the august name of the august child.' The answer was reverently given that the name should be exchanged, and the deity charged: 'To-morrow morning the Heir Apparent must go out on the beach; I will present my thank-offering for the name given me in exchange.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 323-324 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the child went out in the morning, the whole shore was lined with broken-nosed dolphin-fishes. He caused the deity to be addressed: 'Thou bestowest on me fish of thine august food' - and so again his august name was honoured by his being called the Great Deity of August Food, styled today the Food-Wondrous-Great-Deity. The blood from the dolphins' noses stank, so the strand was called Chiura, now Tsunuga.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 323-324 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Oho-sazaki's Answer and the Kohata Maiden
title.zh: 大雀命之對與木幡稚女

region.en: Uji moor, Afumi (Lake Biwa area), Japan

summary.en: Emperor Homuda (Ojin) asks his sons which is dearer, elder or younger child. Oho-sazaki answers that the younger, still a child, is dearer, matching his father's thought; the succession is arranged accordingly. On a progress to Kohata the emperor meets the maiden Miya-nushi-ya-kaha-ye, is entertained in her decorated house, and weds her, singing.
summary.zh: 譽田天皇問二子：長子與次子孰親？大雀命答以年幼之次子為親，暗合天皇之意，遂定傳位之制。後天皇幸近江，於木幡里遇稚女三室屋娘，其父飾屋以待，天皇娶之而歌。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign Homuda asked his sons Oho-yama-mori and Oho-sazaki: 'Which think ye dearer, an elder child or a younger child?' Oho-yama-mori said the elder; Oho-sazaki, divining the feeling behind the question, answered that the elder, already a man, gives no trouble, but the younger, not yet a man, is the dearer. 'My lord Sazaki's words agree with my thoughts,' said the emperor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 330-331 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The inheritance was divided accordingly: Oho-yama-mori to administer the government of the mountains and sea, Oho-sazaki to take charge of the government of the realm, and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko to rule the succession of Heaven's sun - and Oho-sazaki was not disobedient to the commands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 330-331 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, standing on the moor of Uji and gazing at the moor of Kadzu, the emperor sang of the lands spread before him. At the village of Kohata a beautiful maiden met him at a fork in the road: 'I am the daughter of the Grandee Wani-no-Hifure, and my name is Princess Miya-nushi-ya-kaha-ye.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 330-331 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Promising to enter her house on his return, he came the next day; her father, grandly decorating the house, served a great feast, and the maiden presented the great august liquor-cup. The emperor sang in her praise, cohabited with her, and begot the child Uji-no-waki-iratsuko.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 331-333 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Grant of Princess Kami-naga

summary.en: The emperor sends for the beautiful Princess Kami-naga of Himuka; his son the Heir Apparent Oho-sazaki sees her land at Naniwa, falls in love, and begs her through the Prime Minister. The emperor, feasting, sings of the maiden as a mid-tree orange, and bestows her on his son, who sings his joy.
summary.zh: 天皇徵日向縣主之神長媛；太子大雀命見其泊於難波之港，心動，託武內宿禰求之。天皇宴上歌詠少女如橘中實，遂以其女賜太子，太子亦歌以謝。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign, hearing of the beauty of Princess Kami-naga, daughter of the Duke of Muragata in the land of Himuka, thought to employ her at court and sent down for her. Word of the maiden's arrival ran through the palace, and before he could take her for himself, his eldest son saw her first.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 333-335 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the Heir Apparent Oho-sazaki, seeing the maiden land at the port of Naniha and charmed with her grace, directed the Prime Minister, the Noble Take-uchi, to intercede for him, and the Heavenly Sovereign forthwith granted Princess Kami-naga to his august child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 333-335 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: On a day of copious feast the emperor had the maiden present the great august liquor in an oak-leaf to the Heir Apparent, singing that the young girl was as the fragrant orange met by the way, its choicest young fruit in the middle of the tree. Having thus sung, he bestowed her, and the Heir Apparent answered in a song of his own joy and possession.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 334-336 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Korean Tribute to Emperor Ojin: Horses, Analects and Liquor
title.zh: 百濟獻貢：名馬、論語與美酒

summary.en: In Ojin's reign people from Shiragi are set to work on pools; the chieftain of Kudara sends stallion and mare, a cross-sword and a large mirror, then the wise man Wani-kishi with the Confucian Analects and the Thousand Character Essay, smiths and weavers, and the liquor-distiller Susukori - whose sake so excites the emperor that he strikes a stone with his staff and it runs away, giving the proverb 'Hard stones get out of a drunkard's way.'
summary.zh: 譽田天皇之世，新羅人來居而役使，掘百濟池。百濟王肖古獻名馬牝馬各一、橫刀、大鏡；又應求獻賢者王仁，攜《論語》十卷、《千字文》一卷；又獻韓鍛冶卓素、吳織西素。酒司須須許里釀御酒進之，天皇大醉，以杖擊道中大石，石遁走，故諺云：硬石亦避醉人路。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In this reign there came over to Japan people from Shiragi, whom the Noble Take-uchi set to labour on pools and embankments, making the Pool of Kudara. King Shoko, the Chieftain of Kudara, sent as tribute by Achi-kishi one stallion and one mare, and again a cross-sword and likewise a large mirror.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 337-338 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The emperor was graciously bidden by the chieftain to send for a wise man, if there were such in Kudara; he sent Wani-kishi, who brought the Confucian Analects in ten volumes and the Thousand Character Essay in one - altogether eleven volumes. There came too a smith from Kara named Taku-so and a weaver from Go named Sai-so, ancestors of Japan's craftsmen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 338-339 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: There also came the ancestor of the Hada Rulers, the ancestor of the Aya Suzerains, and a man who knew how to distill liquor, Susukori. He distilled great august liquor and presented it; the emperor, excited by it, went out singing - and struck with his august staff a large stone in the middle of the Ohosaka road, upon which the stone ran away. So the proverb says: 'Hard stones get out of a drunkard's way.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 339-340 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Capsized Boat of Oho-yama-mori

region.en: Uji river, Afumi (Lake Biwa area), Japan

summary.en: After Ojin's death, Oho-sazaki cedes the empire to Uji-no-waki-iratsuko, but Oho-yama-mori rebels to slay his younger brother. Uji-no-waki-iratsuko hides on a boat smeared with kudzu slime, feigns to be a common boatman, warns his brother in riddling words that the 'boar' cannot be taken, capsizes the boat, and lets him float down to be shot by archers; a fisherman's feast passed back and forth gives the proverb 'the fisherman weeps over his own things.'
summary.zh: 譽田天皇崩，大雀命讓位於菟道稚郎子，而大山守命不服，欲殺其弟。菟道稚郎子伏兵河畔，於船內敷葛膏使人滑倒，自身扮作船夫；兄登舟問山中有大怒豬否，船夫答：雖百處追逐亦不可得。至河中覆舟，兄浮水而下，伏兵兩岸射之；又以漁師獻膳互讓之事，生諺：漁師自歎己物。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After the decease of the Heavenly Sovereign, Oho-sazaki, in conformity with the commands, ceded the Empire to Uji-no-waki-iratsuko. But Oho-yama-mori, disobeying and anxious to obtain the Empire, had designs to slay the Prince his younger brother, secretly raised an army, and prepared to attack him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 340-341 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Warned, Uji-no-waki-iratsuko set troops in ambush by the river-bank, raised a tent on the hill with a retainer on a throne pretending to be the King, and prepared a boat whose inner grating was rubbed with the slime of pounded kudzu root so that any who trod on it would fall. Putting on a cloth coat and trowsers, he stood in the boat holding the oar, disguised as a common fellow.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 340-341 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The elder King, armour hidden beneath his clothes, was about to board, and asked the boatman: 'It has been reported that on this mountain there is a large and angry boar. Shall I peradventure get that boar?' The answer: 'Thou canst not - he is not to be got however often and wherever chased.' Crossing to mid-river, the prince tilted the boat, and his brother fell into the water and floated down with the current, singing defiance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 341-342 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hidden troops rose on either bank and let their arrows fly; the prince sank at Kawara Point, where searching hooks rang on the armour beneath his clothes. Meanwhile Oho-sazaki and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko kept ceding a fisherman's tribute-feast to one another till the fisherman wept from going back and forwards - whence the proverb, 'the fisherman weeps on account of his own things.' Uji-no-waki-iratsuko died early, and Oho-sazaki ruled the Empire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 342-344 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Ama-no-hi-boko and the Red Jewel

summary.en: A poor girl sleeping on the bank of the Agu lagoon in Shiragi is pierced by rays of the sun and bears a red jewel, which passes to a poor man and is bribed away by the ruler's son Ama-no-hi-boko. The jewel becomes a beautiful wife who, reviled by him, flees by boat to Naniha; Ama-no-hi-boko is barred by the deity of the passage and lands at Tajima, bringing the eight precious treasures: pearls, wave- and wind-shaking and cutting scarves, and mirrors of the offing and shore.
summary.zh: 新羅阿具湖畔貧女晝寢，日光如虹射其私處，遂產赤玉。玉為貧者所持，後被王子天之日矛索去；玉化為美妻，因夫出惡言，乘船逃至難波。日矛追之，為海口神所阻，退泊但馬，攜來珠二串、波振波切風振風切之領巾、沖鏡汀鏡等八寶。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Of old there was a man called Ama-no-hi-boko, child of the ruler of the land of Shiragi, and this was the reason of his crossing to Japan: on the bank of the Agu Lagoon a poor girl was taking her midday sleep when rays of the sun, like a celestial arc, pierced her private parts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 344-345 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: A poor man who watched her strange behaviour saw her, having conceived at that midday sleep, give birth to a red jewel, which he begged, kept wrapped by his side, and later undid to bribe the ruler's son when the man seized him on suspicion of killing a laden cow. Ama-no-hi-boko placed the jewel beside his couch, where it was transformed into a beautiful maiden whom he straightway wedded and made his chief wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 344-345 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The maiden perpetually prepared dainties to feed her husband, till the ruler's child grew proud and reviled her. 'I am not a woman who ought to be the wife of such as thou,' she said; 'I will go to the land of my ancestors' - and secretly she embarked in a boat and fled across to Japan, landing at Naniha.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 345-346 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hearing of his wife's flight, Ama-no-hi-boko crossed in pursuit, but the Deity of the passage prevented his entrance, so he landed in the country of Tajima and stayed there, wedding the daughter of Tajima-no-matawo. The precious treasures he brought over were two strings of pearls, a wave-shaking scarf, a wave-cutting scarf, a wind-shaking scarf, a wind-cutting scarf, a mirror of the offing and a mirror of the shore - eight articles in all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 345-347 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Youth of the Spring Haze and the Wistaria Blossoms

summary.en: Eighty deities woo the Maiden of Idzushi in vain. Two brothers wager for her: the younger, clothed by his mother in wistaria-fibre garments that turn to blossoms, hangs the fragrant bow in the maiden's privy and follows her in to wed her. When the elder refuses to pay the wager, the mother curses him with a brine-soaked bamboo basket so that he withers eight years, then relents at his tears.
summary.zh: 八十神求伊豆志比賣不得。兄弟二人相賭：弟得其母連夜織衣，衣與弓箭皆化藤花，懸於閨側而娶得比賣。兄不償賭物，母怒以竹籠盛鹽石咒之，兄枯萎八年；泣而求赦，母乃解咒復原。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The deity Ama-no-hi-boko had a daughter, the Deity Maiden-of-Idzushi. Eighty deities wished to obtain her in marriage, but none could. At last two brother deities, the Youth-of-the-Glow-on-the-Autumn-Mountains and the Youth-of-the-Haze-on-the-Spring-Mountains, made a wager: if the younger obtained the maiden, the elder would strip off his upper and lower garments, distill liquor in a jar of his own height, and prepare all things of mountain and river as payment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 347-349 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The younger told his mother everything. In a single night she wove and sewed of wistaria-fibre an upper garment, trowsers, socks and boots, made a bow and arrows, and sent him dressed in them to the maiden's house - where all his apparel and weapons turned into wistaria-blossoms.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 348-349 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Youth of the Spring Haze hung the flowering bow and arrows in the maiden's privy; she, finding the blossoms strange, carried them home, and he followed her into the house and forthwith wedded her. She gave birth to a child, and he announced to his elder brother: 'I have obtained the Maiden-of-Idzushi.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 348-349 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Vexed, the elder brother refused to pay the wager. His mother, angry with her elder child, made a coarse basket with eight holes from island bamboo, mixed river stones with brine, wrapped them in the leaves, and had this curse spoken: like the brine flow and ebb, like the stones sink and be prostrate - then placed the basket over the smoke. The elder brother dried up, withered and lay prostrate eight years, till his lamentations moved her to reverse the curse, and his body became sound as before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 349-350 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Nintoku Remits the Taxes; the Reign of the Emperor-Sage
title.zh: 仁德天皇免賦與聖帝之世

summary.en: Emperor Oho-sazaki (Nintoku), dwelling at Takatsu in Naniwa, climbs a high mountain, sees no cooking-smoke anywhere and finds the land poverty-stricken; he remits all taxes and forced labour for three years. His palace leaks rain caught in troughs, yet when smoke is abundant again he resumes exaction, the peasantry prosper, and the reign is praised as that of the Emperor-Sage.
summary.zh: 大雀天皇（仁德）居難波高津宮，登高山望四方，見國中無炊煙，知民貧，遂罷賦稅徭役三年。御殿漏雨以槽承之，不修繕；後見炊煙繁盛，民富而復課，百姓安業，世稱聖帝之政。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: His Augustness Oho-sazaki dwelt in the palace of Takatsu at Naniba and ruled the Empire. In his reign the Kadzuraki, Mibu, Tajihi, Ohokusaka and Wakakusaka Tribes were established as august proxies of his family, people from Hada laboured on the Mamuta embankment and granaries, the Pools of Wani and Yosami were made, and the Naniha and Wobashi channels were dug to lead the rivers to the sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 353-355 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ascending a lofty mountain and looking on the land all round, the Heavenly Sovereign spoke: 'In the whole land there rises no smoke; the land is all poverty-stricken. So I remit all the people's taxes and forced labour from now till three years hence.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 355-356 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Therefore the great palace became dilapidated, the rain leaked in everywhere and no repairs were made; the leaking rain was caught in troughs while the inmates moved to where there was none. Later, looking on the land again, he saw the smoke abundant, found the people rich, and only then exacted taxes and labour; the peasantry prospered and did not suffer. In praise of that august reign it was called the reign of the Emperor-Sage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 355-356 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Princess Kuro Flees the Jealous Empress

summary.en: The Empress Iha-no-hime's jealousy drives the Emperor Nintoku's new favourite, Princess Kuro of Kibi, to flee to her homeland by boat. The emperor pursues her love-sick, singing from a high story and sending men to drive her ashore; under the pretext of viewing Ahaji island he makes a progress to Kibi, where Kuro entertains him plucking cabbage for soup, and they exchange songs.
summary.zh: 磐之媛性妒，仁德天皇新寵吉備之黑姬懼而乘船歸國。天皇於高樓望之而歌，命人驅姬上岸；又詭稱欲觀淡路島，幸吉備，黑姬於山野間採芹作羹奉上，二人相和而歌。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign's Empress, Her Augustness Iha-no-hime, was exceedingly jealous: the concubines could not even peep inside the palace. Hearing of the regular beauty of Princess Kuro, daughter of the Suzerain of Ama in Kibi, the emperor sent for her and employed her; but she, afraid of the Empress's jealousy, fled down to her native land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 356-357 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Gazing from an upper story on Princess Kuro's departure by boat upon the sea, the emperor sang a longing song; the Empress, very angry on hearing it, sent people to the great strand to drive the Princess ashore and chase her away on foot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 356-357 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: For love of her the emperor deceived the Empress, saying he wanted to see the Island of Ahaji; making his progress, he passed on into the land of Kibi. There Princess Kuro grandly lodged him among the mountain-fields and presented great august food; going to where the maiden plucked cabbage to boil into soup, he sang of his love, and she presented songs in reply.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 357-359 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Aralia Leaves of Cape Mitsu and the Reconciliation
title.zh: 御津岬投菜與蟲語和解

summary.en: While the Empress is away plucking aralia leaves, Nintoku weds Yata-no-waki-iratsume. A gossiping coolie tells the news to a lady of her train; the Empress throws the leaves into the sea at Cape Mitsu and goes up to Yamashiro, singing at the camellia trees. Sent to reconcile her, the Grandee Kuchiko is drenched crawling between front and back doors in the rain until her maid, his sister, sings pity; the couple fabricate a tale of strange three-formed insects at Nurinomi's house, and the emperor arrives to sing reconciliation.
summary.zh: 皇后採芹之際，天皇納八田若郎女。膳夫漏言於後列之女，皇后大怒，傾芹菜於海（御津岬），溯河而上幸山城，歌山茶之樹而思君。遣和氣鵠子臣雨中跪求，前門後門皆不得見，其妹鵠日媛歌而泣之；三人共謀以唐人法興寺蟲語掩飾，天皇乃幸筒木，歌而和好。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Empress made a progress to the land of Ki to pluck aralia-leaves for a feast; meanwhile the Heavenly Sovereign wedded Yata-no-waki-iratsume. A coolie from Kozhima in Kibi, on his way home, met a lady of the Empress's train and told her: 'The Heavenly Sovereign has recently wedded Yata-no-waki-iratsume, and plays with her day and night.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 359-360 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Greatly vexed, the Empress threw into the sea all the aralia-leaves aboard her vessel - the place is called Cape Mitsu - and without entering the palace ascended the channel against the current into Yamashiro, singing to the camellia trees of her lord's remembered beauty, and again at the entrance of the Nara mountain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 360-362 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The emperor sent retainers with songs, then the Grandee Kuchiko of Wani; when he prostrated himself at the front door she went out the back, and vice versa, till he crept back and forth on his knees in the pouring rain, the green dye of his garment streaming red. His sister Princess Kuchi, in the Empress's service, sang a pitying song, and the empress asked the reason.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 364-365 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Kuchiko, Kuchi and Nurinomi took counsel and reported that the empress's progress was only to see the strange insects reared by Nurinomi, changing three ways - creeping things, cocoons, flying birds. 'I want to go and see them,' said the emperor, and made a progress up. Standing at the door of her palace he sang reconciliation; the six songs they exchanged that day are the Changing Songs which are Quiet Songs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 365-366 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Queen Medori's Flight to Mount Kurahashi

summary.en: The emperor begs his half-sister Queen Medori through her intended husband King Hayabusa-wake; Medori, despising a sovereign who cannot protect even Yata-no-waki-iratsume from the jealous empress, weds Hayabusa-wake herself. The enraged emperor raises an army; the lovers flee to Mount Kurahashi and are slain at Soni in Uda, and the general who took Medori's jewelled armlet for his own wife is executed by the empress.
summary.zh: 天皇欲求婚於同母妹女鳥王，託隼別王為媒。女鳥王恥天皇不能護八田郎女，遂嫁隼別王而不從命。天皇怒而起兵討殺，二人遁倉椅山而歌，至宇陀忍野被追斬。押勝連取女鳥王腕釧贈己妻，皇后見而斥其辱屍，遂被誅。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign begged for his younger half-sister Queen Medori, using as middle-man his younger brother King Hayabusa-wake. But Medori told him: 'Owing to the violence of the Empress, the Heavenly Sovereign has not deigned to take Yata-no-waki-iratsume into the Palace. So I will not respectfully serve him. I will become the wife of Thine Augustness.' They wedded, and Hayabusa-wake made no report to the emperor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 366-367 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The emperor went straight to Medori's dwelling and stood on the door-sill while she sat at her loom weaving; they exchanged songs, and perceiving her feelings he returned to the palace. When Hayabusa-wake came, his wife sang to him of their pledged love - and the emperor, hearing that song, forthwith raised an army to slay them both.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 367-368 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The lovers fled together and ascended Mount Kurahashi, singing songs of farewell and defiance to the advancing army. When they fled thence and reached Soni in Uda, the Imperial army pursued, overtook, and slew them both there, so that the love sworn at the loom ended under the soldiers' blades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 368-369 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The generalissimo Chief Ohotate of Yamabe took the jewelled armlet from Queen Medori's arm and gave it to his own wife. At the next feast the Empress recognized the armlet on the woman's arm, refused her the liquor-oak-leaf, and summoned the husband: a slave had stripped the armlet from his lady's still-warm body - and Ohotate was put to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 368-369 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Karanu Vessel and the Lute Sounding Seven Miles

region.en: River Tsuki and Awaji island, Japan

summary.en: A tall tree by the river Tsuki throws a shadow that at dawn reaches Ahaji island and at dusk crosses Mount Takayasu; it is cut down into the swift vessel Karanu, used to draw the august water of Ahaji morning and evening. Its broken pieces burn salt, and the leftover wood becomes a lute whose sound re-echoes seven miles.
summary.zh: 月川之西有大樹，朝影至淡路，暮影越高安山。伐之造輕舟，晨昏汲取淡路之水為御水；破板燒鹽，其餘木造琴，其音鳴響七里。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In this august reign there was a tall tree on the west of the river Tsuki. Struck by the morning sun, its shadow reached to the Island of Ahaji; struck by the evening sun, it crossed Mount Takayasu - a tree whose shade spanned the provinces.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 371 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The tree was cut down and made into a vessel - and a very swift-going vessel it was - named Karanu. With it the water of the Island of Ahaji was drawn morning and evening and presented as the great august water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 371 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The broken pieces of the vessel were used as fuel to burn salt, and the leftover wood was made into a lute whose sound re-echoed seven miles off - so someone sang of its saya-saya ring answering the wet sea-plants of Yura. Thus one tree became vessel, salt-fire, and sounding lute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 371-372 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Richuu's Burning Palace and Sobakari's Reward
title.zh: 履中天皇宮火與曾婆加理之賞

summary.en: While Emperor Iza-ho-wake (Richuu) sleeps drunk at a feast in Naniha, his brother King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu fires the palace; the Suzerain of Achi carries him off on horseback to Yamato. His brother Midzu-ha-wake (Hanzei) is ordered to prove loyalty by killing the arsonist: he bribes the guardsman Sobakari, who spears his king in the privy, and at the reward banquet Midzu-ha-wake cuts off the regicide's head with a sabre hidden under the matting.
summary.zh: 履中天皇宴於難波，醉寢，弟墨江中王縱火焚宮。阿知都王偷載天皇乘馬逃入大和，一路作歌。弟水齒別命奉命殺墨江中王以自明：賄其衛士曾婆加理，於廁中以矛弒之。行賞之宴，水齒別命預置劍於席下，趁賜爵之酒覆面，斬其首。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Originally, when dwelling at the palace of Naniha, the Heavenly Sovereign Iza-ho-wake, intoxicated with the great august liquor at a great tasting, fell greatly asleep. His younger brother, King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu, wishing to take the throne, set fire to the great palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 373 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Suzerain of Achi, ancestor of the Aya Suzerains of Yamato, took the emperor away by stealth, set him on an august horse and made him progress into Yamato. Waking at the moor of Tajihi, the emperor learned of the fire and sang of the flames still bright at Naniha; at the Ohosaka mountain a woman warned him that armed men barred the way, so he went round by Tagima and dwelt in the temple of the Deity of Isonokami.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 373-375 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: His brother Midzu-ha-wake came for an audience, and was told: 'I am in doubt whether perhaps you may not be of like mind with King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu. Return down and slay him, and come up again; then I will surely meet and speak with thee.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 375-376 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Midzu-ha-wake bribed the man-at-arms Sobakari with the promise of the Prime Ministership; Sobakari watched his king enter the privy and thrust him to death with a spear. At a halt and sudden feast at the mountain entrance the King bestowed the promised rank, then - while the great cup hid the traitor's drinking face - drew a sabre laid under the matting and cut off his head, judging that one who had slain his lord could not be suffered to live; the place was called Chika-tsu-Asuka. Going up to Isonokami he reported the deed done, and was received.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 376-377 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Ingyou's Cure and the Hot-Water Trial of Surnames
title.zh: 允恭天皇療疾與湯沸定姓

summary.en: Wo-asa-dzu-ma-waku-go (Ingyou), long sick, at first declines the throne; the ruler of Shiragi dutifully sends eighty-one tribute vessels whose chief envoy, deeply versed in medicine, cures him. To end the confusion of false surnames and gentile names, he sets jars of boiling water at the Wondrous Cape of Eighty Evils in Words at Amakashi and settles the surnames of the eighty heads of companies by ordeal.
summary.zh: 雄朝津間稚子宿禰天皇（允恭）久病辭位，新羅獻貢船八十一艘，其大使妙於醫術，醫愈天皇之疾。又患天下氏姓錯亂，於甘樫丘之誓湯丘設沸湯之鼎，令八十氏族長就湯以定氏姓。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign Wo-asa-dzu-ma-waku-go-no-sukune dwelt in the Palace of Toho-tsu-Asuka and ruled the Empire. When first about to rule the succession of Heaven's Sun, he declined, saying: 'I have a long sickness; I cannot rule the sun's succession' - but from the Empress downwards all the magnates strongly urged him, and he forthwith ruled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 379-380 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: At this time the ruler of Shiragi dutifully sent eighty-one vessels with august tribute across the sea. The chief envoy who accompanied the tribute, Komu-ha-chimu-kamu-ki-mu, was a man deeply versed in the medical art, and with his skill he cured the Heavenly Sovereign's august sickness - the long illness that had made him refuse the throne was healed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 380 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Lamenting the transgressions in the surnames and gentile names of the people - many claiming names that were not theirs - the emperor placed jars for trial by hot water at the Wondrous Cape of Eighty Evils in Words at Amakashi, and deigned to establish by ordeal the surnames and gentile names of the eighty heads of companies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 380-381 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Karu and the Great Lady of Karu: Banishment and Double Death
title.zh: 輕皇子與輕大娘皇女：流放與殉死

summary.en: Chosen to succeed but discovered to have debauched his younger sister, the Great Lady of Karu, the Heir Apparent Karu of Ki-nashi loses all support to Prince Anaho, flees, is besieged and surrendered by the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe, and is banished to the hot waters of Iyo. The Queen So-tohoshi follows him out of love, and when she at last reaches him they sing and kill themselves together.
summary.zh: 草香幡梭皇子之妹輕大娘皇女（衣通姬）之美動天下。輕皇子與其妹私通，事聞，眾叛而歸安康王。輕皇子遁於忍馬屋小前老女之家被圍，由大前小前宿禰獻出，流放伊予溫泉。衣通姬追之不得，二人相會而歌，遂同時自殺。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: After the decease of the Heavenly Sovereign it was settled that King Karu of Ki-nashi should rule the Sun's succession. But in the interval before his accession he debauched his younger sister the Great Lady of Karu, singing proud rustic songs of sleeping well whatever people might plot against him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 382-383 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Therefore all the officials and likewise the people of the Empire turned from the Heir Apparent Karu to the August Child Anaho. Karu, alarmed, fled into the house of the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe and made implements of war; Anaho likewise, raised an army, and beleaguered the house, singing through the heavy ice-rain at the gate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 383-384 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe came dancing and singing, 'Come not with arms against the King thine elder brother - people will surely laugh. I will secure him and present him to thee.' Anaho disbanded his troops; the noble secured Prince Karu, presented him, and the captive prince was banished to the hot waters of Iyo, singing on the road of the mats he might not defile and of his sister whom he loved like a true jewel and a mirror.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 384-386 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Queen So-tohoshi presented a song to the banished prince, and being unable to restrain her love went after him. When she reached the place where he pensively waited he sang: if they said his sister, whom he loved like a true jewel, were there, he would go home and long for his country - and having thus sung, they forthwith killed themselves together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 387-389 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Child King Mayowa Avenges His Father
title.zh: 安康天皇與稚子熊娃之復仇

summary.en: The Grandee of Ne steals the jewel headdress sent as a gift by King Oho-kusaka and slanders him, so the Heavenly Sovereign Anaho slays Oho-kusaka and takes his wife as empress. Warning his drowsing empress that he fears her son Mayowa will one day avenge his father, the emperor is overheard by the seven-year-old boy himself, who watches until Anaho sleeps and cuts off his head with the great sword, then flees to the Grandee Tsubura.
summary.zh: 根臣竊取大草香皇子所獻印齒珠而讒之，穴穗天皇遂殺大草香皇子，奪其妻為后。后携前夫之子稚子熊娃居宮中。天皇語后：「吾懼其子長大知我弒其父而復仇。」時七歲稚子熊娃在廊下聞之，俟帝晝寢，取大刀斬帝首，逃入平群臣之家。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign sent the Grandee of Ne to King Oho-kusaka on behalf of his younger brother Prince Oho-hatsuse, to command the presentation of the King's younger sister Queen Waka-kusaka in marriage. Oho-kusaka dutifully promised her and sent back, as a ceremonial gift for the emperor, a push-wood jewel headdress.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 390 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Grandee of Ne stole the jewel headdress and slandered the King, reporting that Oho-kusaka had refused the Imperial Commands and grasped his sword in anger. The Heavenly Sovereign, in great anger, slew King Oho-kusaka, took that King's chief wife Nagata-no-oho-iratsume, and made her Empress.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 390 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sleeping at midday, the emperor asked his Empress what was on her mind, and she answered nothing - for her former husband's child, King Ma-yowa, seven years old, was playing just outside the apartment. Not knowing the boy could hear, the emperor said: 'I have constantly something upon my mind - the fear that thy child King Ma-yowa, when he comes to man's estate and learns that I slew the King his father, will requite me with a foul heart.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 391 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The child caught the words, watched for the Heavenly Sovereign to be augustly asleep, took the great sword that lay at his side, struck off his head, and fled into the house of the Grandee Tsubura. Thus the wronged orphan avenged his father's blood before he was old enough to fear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 391 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Ohohatsuse Seizes the Throne

summary.en: Told of Anaho's murder, the lad Oho-hatsuse strangles his unconcerned elder brother Kuro-biko and buries his brother Shiro-biko alive up to the loins; he then besieges the Grandee Tsubura, whose loyal speech ends with the prince's death and Tsubura's own suicide. On a Afumi moor he ambushes King Oshiha under his clothes, shoots him, cuts up the body into a horse's manger, and the orphaned princes Ohoke and Woke flee into Harima as grooms.
summary.zh: 雄略（大泊瀨）聞天皇遇弑，責兄黑彥王冷漠而扼殺之，又活埋白彥王於畝旁。圍平群臣之家，平群臣力戰不支，殺皇子與己身以殉。又獵近江蒲原野，甲胄伏於衣內，突射殺其兄意祁王，碎屍納馬槽而埋之。意祁王之子億計王、弘計王亡命播磨，為馬夫牧童。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Prince Oho-hatsuse, then a lad, was grieved and furious at the murder of the Heavenly Sovereign, and went to his elder brother King Kuro-biko: 'They have slain the Heavenly Sovereign. What shall be done?' Kuro-biko was not startled but unconcerned - so Oho-hatsuse clutched him by the collar, dragged him out, drew his sword, and slew him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 392-393 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: His other elder brother King Shiro-biko showed the same unconcern; Oho-hatsuse clutched him too, and on reaching Woharida dug a pit and buried him standing, so that when he was buried to the loins both his eyes burst out and he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 392-393 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Raising an army, he beleaguered the house of the Grandee Tsubura, who sheltered both Mayowa and the maiden Princess Kara. Arrows fell like reeds; Tsubura came forth unarmed and offered the princess and five granaries, declaring that grandees hide in kings' palaces, but kings do not hide in grandees' houses, and a loyal slave must die rather than desert a prince who trusted him. When their strength and arrows were spent, the prince begged death: Tsubura thrust the prince through with his sword and then cut off his own head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 393-394 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Told of boars and deer in abundance at Kuta on the moor of Kaya in Afumi, Oho-hatsuse went hunting with King Ichi-no-be-no-oshiha. Warned that Oshiha was a violent-spoken prince, he put armour under his clothes, girded bow and arrows, rode level with the other king in a sudden interval, shot Oshiha down, cut his body to pieces, put them into a horse's manger, and buried them level with the earth. Oshiha's children, Kings Ohoke and Woke, fled across Yamashiro and the River Kusuba into Harima, where an old tattooed boar-herd once seized their provisions - and they hid in a native's house, working as grooms and cow-herds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 394-395 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Raised-Roof House and the White Dog

summary.en: Progressing through Kafuchi, Emperor Oho-hatsuse sees a subject's house built with a raised roof-frame like his own and has it set on fire; the trembling lord offers a white dog clothed in cloth with a bell round its neck, and the burning is stopped. The emperor then sends the strange dog as a wooing-gift to Queen Waka-kusaka-be, who answers that she will come up to serve him, and he sings to her of intertwined bamboos not yet entwined.
summary.zh: 雄略天皇幸河內，見志紀縣主屋頂作懸屋，怒曰：賤奴僭擬御殿！命焚其屋。縣主戰懼獻白狗，披布繫鈴；天皇乃止焚，又以白狗為聘，遣人致若草香部郎女。郎女答曰：背日臨幸可畏，吾將上京奉仕。天皇登歌於山而詠之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In the beginning, when the Empress dwelt at Kusaka, the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress into Kafuchi by way of the Tadagoye road. Climbing a mountain-top and gazing over the country, he saw a house built with a raised roof-frame, and asked whose it was: 'It is the house of the great Departmental Lord of Shiki.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 397-398 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'What! a slave builds his own house in imitation of the august abode of the Heavenly Sovereign!' - and he forthwith sent men to burn the house down. The Great Departmental Lord, trembling and bowing his head, pleaded that being a slave he had built overmuch in ignorance, and presented as an offering of entreaty a white dog clothed in cloth with a bell hung round its neck, led by a string by his kinsman Koshihaki. The emperor ordered the burning to desist.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 397-398 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Making a progress to the residence of Queen Waka-kusaka-be, he sent the dog as a present with the message that this strange thing got on the road was a thing to woo with. She answered that it was very alarming he should come with his back to the sun, so she would come up straight to the capital and respectfully serve him - and the emperor, standing on the mountain ascent, sang to his beloved of bamboos not yet intertwined.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 398-399 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Akawi-ko: Eighty Years' Vigil at the Miwa River
title.zh: 引田部赤猪子八十年待命

summary.en: By the river Miwa the emperor meets the beautiful Akawi-ko of the Hiketa Tribe washing clothes and forbids her to marry: 'I will send for thee.' Eighty years she reverently awaits the summons; grown lean and withered, she comes up with a hundred tables of merchandise to show her faithfulness. The emperor, startled and pitiful, cannot wed her aged form but confers on her songs of the sacred dwelling, and sends her back plentifully endowed.
summary.zh: 雄略天皇幸三輪川，見美少女引田部赤猪子浣衣，命勿嫁，曰：吾將召汝。赤猪子待命八十年，形容枯槁，乃陳百几之調物以表忠貞。天皇愕然而憐之，欲娶而嫌其老，遂賜御歌而厚贈遣歸。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Once when the Heavenly Sovereign went out for amusement and reached the River Miwa, there was a girl of very beautiful aspect washing clothes by the river-side. Asked whose child she was, she answered: 'My name is Akawi-ko of the Hiketa Tribe.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 399-400 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The emperor caused her to be told: 'Do not thou marry a husband. I will send for thee,' and returned to the palace. Eighty years passed while she reverently awaited the Heavenly Sovereign's commands; then, thinking her face and form lean and withered and hope gone, yet unable to bear hiding her faithfulness, she caused merchandise on a hundred tables to be carried and came forth to present it as tribute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 400-401 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The emperor, who had quite forgotten the command of long ago, asked what old woman she was. She declared how in such a month of such a year she had received his command and waited eighty years, her prime passed away in vain. 'This is very pitiful,' he said; in his heart he wished to marry her, but shrank from her extreme age, and instead conferred on her an august song.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 400-401 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the great august song the tears that Akawi-ko wept quite drenched the red-dyed sleeve she wore, and in reply she sang songs of her own unchangeable faith - that for every reason it had been impossible for her ever to give her affections to another, and that she had come up to the capital to demonstrate to him who had forgotten her the constancy of her heart. Then the old woman was sent back plentifully endowed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 401-402 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dancer of Yeshinu

summary.en: Progressing to Yeshinu the emperor weds a beautiful girl of the river bank. On a later visit he raises a great august throne on the very spot of their meeting, seats himself, plays his lute, and makes the maiden dance; for her good dancing he composes an august song in her praise.
summary.zh: 雄略天皇幸吉野，娶川畔美少女。再幸其地，即舊逢處設御座，自彈琴而令女舞；嘉其舞之善，作歌贊之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress to the palace of Yeshinu, there was on the bank of the Yeshinu river a girl of beautiful appearance. Having wedded this girl he returned to the Palace, but the meeting-place by the river stayed in his memory through the seasons that followed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 402 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Afterwards, when he again made a progress to Yeshinu, he halted where he had first met the girl, raised a great august throne in that place, seated himself upon it, played on his august lute, and made the maiden dance.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 402 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: For the maiden's good dancing he composed an august song in her praise, wedding the memory of their first meeting to the music of the lute in the river valley. Thus the emperor of the age made of one riverside encounter a royal romance, a dance, and a song that kept her name alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 402-403 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dragonfly that Named Akitsushima

region.en: Moor of Akidzu, Yamato (Nara), Japan (symbolic pin)

summary.en: Hunting from his throne on the moor of Akidzu, the emperor is bitten on the arm by a horse-fly; a dragonfly at once comes, eats up the horse-fly, and flies away. He composes a song of thanks, and from that time the moor is called Akidzu-nu - whence Akitsushima, Dragonfly Island, the poetic name of Japan itself.
summary.zh: 雄略天皇於秋津野御座而獵，牛虻齧其臂，忽有蜻蛉飛來啖虻而去。天皇作歌謝之，其野遂名秋津洲，日本之雅稱由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress to the Moor of Akidzu and augustly hunted, he sat on an august throne. A horse-fly bit his august arm, and forthwith a dragonfly came and ate up the horse-fly, and flew away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 403 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Thereupon he composed an august song in thanks for the dragonfly's service, for the insect had avenged the august arm of the sovereign with a sudden flash of wings. From that time that moor was called by the name of Akidzu-nu, the Dragonfly Moor, and the hunters remembered the song as long as they walked the field.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 403-404 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the moor's name comes Akitsushima, the Island of the Dragon-fly - the poetic name of Japan itself. The commentators even reversed the common assumption: it was not the island that was called after Japan, but Japan that was called after the dragon-fly, so that the country's loveliest old name was born from one small winged avenger on a hunting morning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 404 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Boar of Kadzuraki and the Deity Lord of One Word

summary.en: On Mount Kadzuraki a wounded boar roars back at the emperor, who climbs an alder and sings. On a later progress a retinue exactly like his own - garments, red cords, order of march - ascends the opposite acclivity; arrows are fixed on both sides until the other declares himself the Great Deity of Kadzuraki, Lord of One Word, who dispels evil and good with a word. The emperor strips his hundred officials of their garments as offerings, and the deity escorts him down the mountain.
summary.zh: 雄略天皇射葛城山豬，豬怒吼反撲，帝懼而登榿木而歌。又幸葛城山，見對山上人馬服飾與御仗儀仗無異；兩軍張弓相峙，對方自報：吾乃一言主神，善言則善、惡言則惡之神。天皇戰慄致敬，脫百官衣裳并自佩弓劍進獻，神擊掌受之，且送帝至葛城山麓。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Once the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress up to the summit of Mount Kadzuraki, and a large wild boar ran out. He shot it with a whizzing barb, but the boar, furious, came towards him roaring; alarmed at the roaring, he climbed up to the top of an alder and sang there of his peril and the mercy of his great lord.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 404-405 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Again, on a progress up Mount Kadzuraki, all the officials were clothed in green-stained garments with red cords. On the opposite mountain acclivity people ascended quite similar to the order of the Heavenly Monarch's retinue - the habiliments and the very people indistinguishable. 'There being no other king in Yamato excepting myself,' the emperor demanded, 'what person goeth thus?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 405-406 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Very angry, he fixed his arrow, and the officials all fixed theirs - and those people also fixed their arrows. 'Let each tell his name, and then let fly his arrow.' The reply: 'I was the first to be asked, I will be the first to tell my name. I am the deity who dispels with a word the evil and with a word the good - the Great Deity of Kadzuraki, Lord of One Word.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 405-406 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign trembled and reverenced the Great Deity; beginning with his great august sword and bow and arrows, he took off the garments of the hundred officials and worshipfully presented them, and the Deity, clapping his hands, accepted the offering. Descending the mountain, the Great Deity respectfully escorted the emperor to the entrance of the Hatsuse mountain - so it was that the Lord of One Word was revealed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 406 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Leaf in the Liquor Cup and the Maid of Mihe
title.zh: 盃中落葉與三女汀采女

summary.en: Going to wed Princess Wodo of Kasuga, the emperor sees a girl hide behind a mound and sings of digging her out with five hundred metal spades - whence the Mound of the Metal Spade. At a feast under a hundred-branching tsuki-tree, a leaf falls into the liquor-cup of the maid from Mihe, and he is about to cut off her head; her inspired song of the sacred palace and the falling leaves wins pardon, and she is praised and plentifully endowed.
summary.zh: 雄略天皇幸春日欲婚幡梭郎女，途中少女匿於塚畔，帝歌以五百鐵鍬掘山取之，其塚遂名鐵鍬塚。又於初瀨百枝木下大宴，三女汀采女奉杯，落葉浮於盃中；帝拔劍欲斬，采女歌詠日御門與建木之靈義而得赦，大加褒賞。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Again when the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress to Kasuga to wed Princess Wodo, daughter of the Grandee Satsuki of Wani, a maiden met him by the way, and, seeing the Imperial progress, ran and hid on the side of a mound. The emperor composed an august song, jesting that he desired five hundred metal spades like hers wherewith to break down the hill-side and dig her out - and so that mound was called the Mound of the Metal Spade.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 406-407 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he made a copious feast under a hundred-branching tsuki-tree at Hatsuse, a female attendant from Mihe in the land of Ise lifted up the great august cup and presented it to him. From the tree there fell a leaf and floated in the great august cup; not knowing it, the maid did not desist from presenting the liquor, but the emperor, perceiving the leaf, knocked her down, put his sword to her neck, and was about to cut off her head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 407-408 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Slay me not! There is something that I must say to thee,' the maid cried, and sang: the palace of Hishiro at Makimuku shines with the morning and evening sun, and on the hundred-fold flourishing tsuki-tree the leaves fall from branch to branch into the fresh jewelled goblet, curdle-curdle - a very awful thing, August Child of the High-Shining Sun, and the tradition of the thing, too, this!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 407-408 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her song of heavenly words recalled how drops of brine that fell curdling became the first island of the archipelago - so that a leaf falling into liquor must be a good omen rather than a crime. The emperor sang in reply, and at that copious feast the female attendant from Mihe was praised and plentifully endowed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 409-411 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fire-Tenders' Dance in Harima

summary.en: After Seinei's death the realm seeks a king and finds Princess Ihi-toyo. Wodate, newly appointed governor of Harima, comes to the new-cave rejoicing of Shizhimu, where two young fire-tending children dance with princely courtesy, each yielding precedence to the other. The younger's chant of the red-painted sword and banners hidden among the bamboos reveals them as beggarly descendants of emperors - the hidden princes Ohoke and Woke, whose father Ichinobe was slain.
summary.zh: 清寧天皇崩而無嗣，求飯豐王女為主。山背守小楯宿禰幸播磨志染神社新屋大宴，二灶童相讓起舞；弟詠赤旗之劍藏於竹叢之歌，自曝為乞食流亡之皇孫，即億計、弘計二王。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign Shiraka-no-oho-yamato-ne-ko had no Empress and no august children; after his decease there was no King to rule the Empire, and enquiry was made for one to rule the sun's succession. Wodate, Chief of the Mountain Clan, was appointed governor of the land of Harima, and arrived just at the time of a rejoicing for the new cave of an inhabitant called Shizhimu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 413-414 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the feasting and drinking were at their height, all danced in turns; two young children employed to light the fire sat beside the furnace, and were made to dance. 'Do thou the elder brother dance first.' 'Do thou the younger brother dance first.' Laughing at their mutual yielding, the assembly waited till the elder at last danced; then, when the younger was about to dance, he chanted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 414-415 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chant spoke of a sword painted and decorated with red streamers, of red banners hidden behind the thick leaves of the bamboo-grove - as the Imperial origin of the two young princes was hidden beneath the vile office they filled in Shizhimu's household - and ended with the words 'beggarly descendants,' by which the singer revealed his own and his brother's princely birth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 415-416 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: The Song-Hedge Quarrel with the Grandee Shibi

summary.en: As the two princes are about to assume rule, the Grandee Shibi seizes in a song-hedge the maiden Ofuwo whom Prince Woke is about to wed, and taunts him with tunny-metaphors in alternating songs. The princes resolve that no better time to act can come than when the Grandee's gate stands empty of men, raise an army, besiege and slay Shibi, and then cede the empire to one another until the younger Woke rules first.
summary.zh: 二王將即位，平群臣志比於歌垣中奪弘計王將娶之乙媛，以鰹魚之喻相譏相和。王等伺志比宅門無人，舉兵圍而殺之。既而兄弟互讓帝位，弟弘計王以兄讓而先即位。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When the government of the Empire was about to be assumed, the Grandee Shibi, ancestor of the Grandees of Heguri, mixed in the Songs and took the hand of the beautiful person whom Prince Woke was about to wed - the maiden Ofuwo, daughter of one of the Headmen of Uda. Woke likewise mixed in the Song-Hedge, and they taunted one another in alternating songs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 416-418 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Song answered song in growing anger: the prince likened himself to a fisherman who would fain spear the great tunny, the Grandee jeered at the dilapidated palace and the sorry fortunes of the princes, and the war of words mounted to threats of cutting and burning one another's houses down.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 417-419 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The princes took counsel together: 'Unless it be now, it were hard to plot against him, for there is nobody at the gate' - and forthwith they raised an army, beleaguered the house of the Grandee Shibi, and slew him, ending the song-hedge rivalry with spears instead of verses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 418-419 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then each of the two Princes ceded the Empire to the other. Ohoke urged: 'Had not Thine Augustness revealed our names when we dwelt in the house of Shizhimu in Harima, we should never have arrived at being the lords of the Empire. Though I be the elder brother, do Thine Augustness rule first.' Unable to refuse, His Augustness Woke ruled the Empire first.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 419-420 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Emperor Woke Finds His Father's Bones
title.zh: 顯宗天皇尋父骨與老嫗置目

summary.en: Emperor Woke, searching for the august bones of his murdered father King Ichinobe, receives a poor old woman from Afumi who alone knows the grave - and can tell the skeleton by its teeth. The bones are dug up, interred in a new mausoleum, and the old woman, named Oki-me, is housed beside the palace and summoned daily by a bell; when she begs to go home the emperor sees her off with songs.
summary.zh: 顯宗天皇弘計求其父市之邊王之骨。近江有一老嫗自言知埋骨處，且能以齒辨之。發土得骨，葬於蒲原野東山陵，使賀富臣子孫守之。天皇召嫗入宮，賜名置目，宮畔築屋，擊鈴而召之；後老嫗乞歸鄉，天皇賜歌送之。

passages.text: His Augustness Woke-no-ihasu-wake dwelt at the palace of Chika-tsu-Asuka and ruled the Empire. At the time when the Heavenly Sovereign was searching for the august bones of the King his father, King Ichinobe, there came out from the land of Afumi to the palace a poor old woman, who said: 'The place where the prince's august bones are buried is specially well known to me, and moreover his skeleton can be known by his august teeth.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 419-420 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: People were set to dig the ground and search; the bones were forthwith obtained, an august mausoleum was made on the mountain east of the Moor of Kaya, and they were interred there, with the children of Kara-fukuro set to guard it. Afterwards the august bones were brought up to the Capital.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 419-420 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The emperor sent for the old woman, praised her for having kept the place in mind without forgetting, and conferred on her the name of the Old Woman Oki-me. He built her a house close to the palace, always sent for her every day, hung a bell by the door of the great hall, and always rang it when he wished to call her, singing a song of her long journey from valley and moor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 420-421 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old woman said she was very aged and would fain depart to her native land; the Heavenly Sovereign let her depart according to her request, saw her off, and sang a farewell song of the hundred stages by which she had come.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 421 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: Woke's Vengeance on the Herdman and the Mausoleum

region.en: Asuka river and Mozu mound (Nara/Osaka), Japan

summary.en: The boar-herd who seized the princes' provisions in their days of flight is hunted out, beheaded in the bed of the river Asuka, and all his kindred have their knee-tendons cut, so his descendants limp to this day when they come up to Yamato. Wishing revenge on the spirit of Yuryaku, Woke would demolish his mausoleum; his brother Ohoke undertakes the deed, only slightly excavating its side, arguing that an emperor's tomb must be spared while the insult suffices as a token to future ages.
summary.zh: 顯宗天皇尋得昔日奪食之野豬飼夫，斬於飛鳥川之原，並刳其族人之膝筋，故其子孫至今上大和而自跛。又欲掘雄略天皇之陵以報父仇；兄億計王自任其事，僅微掘陵側而還，奏曰：叔父雖為父仇，然曾君臨天下，盡毀其陵恐遭後世非議，微掘以為後世之鑒足矣。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Heavenly Sovereign searched for the old boar-herd who had seized his august provisions at the time when he first met with adversity and was fleeing; having sought him out, he sent for him up to the Capital, beheaded him in the bed of the River Asuka, and cut the knee-tendons of all his kindred. Wherefore down to the present time his descendants, on the day when they come up to Yamato, always limp of their own accord; the man's abode had been well seen and divined, so the place was named Shimesu.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 421-422 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Deeply hating the Heavenly Sovereign Oho-hatsuse, who had slain the King his father, the emperor wished to be revenged on his spirit by destroying his august mausoleum. His elder brother Ohoke addressed him: 'To demolish this august mausoleum thou shouldst not send other people. None but myself shall go.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 422-423 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ohoke proceeded down, slightly excavated the side of the mausoleum, and reported the deed done. Challenged on his quick return, he explained: revenge on their father's foe is just, but Oho-hatsuse was still their uncle and a Heavenly Sovereign who ruled the Empire - to demolish wholly the mausoleum of a ruler would be reviled by after-generations, so a slight excavation will suffice as a token to future ages. 'This also is very just,' said the emperor, and let it be.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 422-423 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

title.en: No Heir: Keitai Sent For and the Revolt of Ihawi
title.zh: 繼體天皇入繼與磐余之叛

summary.en: Emperor Buretsu dies childless, leaving no prince to inherit; Ohoda, fifth descendant of Emperor Homuda, is sent for from Afumi, married to Princess Tashiraka, and presented with the Empire, ruling from the palace of Tamaho. In his reign Ihawi, Lord of Tsukushi, defies the imperial decrees, and the Great Chieftain Mononobe-no-arakawi and the Chieftain Ohotomo-no-kanamura are both sent to slay him.
summary.zh: 武烈天皇崩而無嗣，乃迎近江之彥太（繼體天皇，譽田天皇五世孫），婚於手白香皇女，奉以帝位，居磐余玉穰宮。其世筑紫國造磐井不遵朝命，大逆無道，乃遣物部麁鹿火大連與大伴金村連俱誅之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese court myth (Kojiki); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: His Grandeur Wo-hatsuse-no-waka-sazaki dwelt in the palace of Namiki at Hatsuse and ruled the Empire for eight years, having no august children; the Wo-hatsuse Tribe was established as his august proxy. On his death there was no prince anywhere to inherit the Empire, and the imperial line itself seemed about to fail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 424 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: So His Augustness Ohoda, the fifth descendant of the Heavenly Monarch Homuda, was sent for down from the land of Afumi, married to Her Augustness Tashiraka, and presented with the Empire. Dwelling in the Palace of Tamaho at Ihare, he ruled as the Heavenly Sovereign Keitai.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource pages 424-425 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.

passages.text: In this august reign Ihawi, Lord of Tsukushi, was disobedient to the Imperial Decrees and was exceedingly disrespectful. So the Great Chieftain Mononobe-no-arakawi and the Chieftain Ohotomo-no-kanamura were both sent to slay Ihawi - the lord of the great clans going together against the rebel of the western road.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kojiki, Wikisource page 425 (trans. Chamberlain 1882); not verbatim.
